content: 1. When linking HIV prevention data systems to other clinical datasets, such as those for HIV treatment, it is essential to ensure the protection of personal identifiers to maintain confidentiality and data security. 2. Chapter 3 emphasizes the importance of person-centered HIV patient monitoring to enhance testing, early diagnosis, and treatment. It recommends promoting the analysis and use of routinely collected testing data to optimize HIV testing services, particularly in populations and settings with a high proportion of undiagnosed individuals living with HIV. This approach supports early diagnosis and treatment initiation. 3. Monitoring the time to HIV diagnosis should be improved to facilitate rapid antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and engagement in care, thereby reducing morbidity and mortality. 4. The use of person-centered patient data is recommended to continuously assess interruptions in HIV treatment, aiming to improve re-engagement and retention in care. Strengthening routine data analysis can help identify treatment interruptions and support interventions to re-initiate ART and re-engage patients in care. 5. Longitudinal monitoring of individuals on ART is recommended by linking data across services through improved referral systems, follow-up mechanisms, and integrated service delivery. 6. Standardized and digitized tools should be used in health facilities and community-delivered services to optimize data collection, reporting, and flow for linkage and monitoring purposes. 7. Data collection and reporting for differentiated service delivery in HIV patient monitoring systems should be integrated and strengthened to improve treatment outcomes and programmatic efficiency. This includes linking community-delivered services to health facilities while ensuring that clinical care and follow-up remain the responsibility of health facilities. 8. The impact of differentiated service delivery on treatment outcomes, such as retention, viral load suppression, and program efficiency, should be monitored. This includes evaluating reduced clinical visits and staff time. 9. Routine data quality assessments should be included in long-term data quality improvement processes to strengthen data use and improve HIV treatment outcomes. This involves integrating assessments of HIV treatment and viral load testing data quality with broader data quality improvement efforts. 10. Enhanced data analysis, frequent feedback to data custodians and users, standardized information products, and mentorship and training should be supported to improve treatment outcomes and service delivery. 11. Aggregated, de-duplicated individual-level patient treatment data should be used to inform drug inventory management, dispensing, procurement, and logistics at national, district, and facility levels. This approach reduces drug wastage and stockouts. 12. Chapter 4 highlights the integration of related infections into HIV surveillance systems. Person-centered data should support improved health and quality of life over a lifetime, with routine HIV systems monitoring related infections such as tuberculosis (TB), sexually transmitted infections (STIs), hepatitis B and C, pre-invasive cervical disease, cancer, and non-communicable diseases. 13. STI testing and treatment should be measured as part of HIV prevention, testing, and treatment programs. 14. Recent records of STI symptoms, diagnoses, or treatment should be included in HIV data systems as key events to trigger HIV testing and prevention services. 15. Hepatitis B and C testing and treatment services should be provided and measured as part of HIV prevention, testing, and treatment programs, particularly among people living with HIV and priority populations such as people who inject drugs, sex workers, men who have sex with men, and individuals in prisons or other closed settings. 16. Screening and treatment for cervical cancer are recommended and should be recorded in routine HIV reporting systems to monitor services received by women living with HIV. 17. Chapter 5 focuses on harnessing routine data for HIV surveillance. National health information systems should include and strengthen individual-level HIV surveillance that routinely links data on HIV prevention, diagnosis, and treatment over time as individuals move between facilities and locations. 18. A minimum dataset of routine clinical health information should be collected for national surveillance to monitor and guide the HIV response and support the measurement of incidence. Person-centered data methods, such as back-calculation and retesting, should be considered alongside other data sources and modeling to improve incidence measurement. 19. CD4 testing at HIV diagnosis is recommended for clinical staging, providing information on entry or re-entry to care, and estimating HIV incidence. 20. Mortality and causes of death (AIDS-related and non-AIDS-related) should be reported for all individuals registered in routine HIV information systems. Vital registration records should be consulted to measure the overall burden of AIDS mortality, including as a proportion of total deaths. 21. Expanding and strengthening HIV case surveillance systems using simple electronic interfaces and built-in validation mechanisms is recommended to better capture new HIV diagnoses and risk factors for HIV acquisition. 22. Chapter 6 addresses digital health data interoperability. Interoperability standards, data use rules, obligations, and transparent data governance should be explicitly built into digital health systems to enable secure exchange and use of health data. 23. Technical, organizational, and legal interoperability standards should be used to facilitate data governance and smooth data exchange and use between healthcare sector partners. 24. Agreed-upon standards, rules, frameworks, and conditions for data use should be published by health ministries, partners, and civil society to improve transparency, data sharing, and use. 25. Unique identifiers that replace names and personal information with anonymous alphanumeric codes should be used to support person-centered data, enabling individuals to access services over time and across facilities, districts, and health programs. 26. Unique identifiers should be supported by data protection policies to preserve individual anonymity, separating personal and confidential data from routinely shared health data. 27. Unique identifiers should be progressively introduced across facilities, districts, disease programs, and other healthcare settings to promote person-centered services. 28. National technical and legal protections should be adopted for individuals' unique identifiers, allowing them to access data associated with their identifiers. 29. Investments should be made in secure and confidential data systems protected by policies and rights, with different data security levels for various data elements and healthcare users. 30. Personal data should remain confidential and accessible only to the data subject and explicitly authorized parties. 31. Security measures should include suitable policies and regulations, not just technical security. 32. Patients should have access to their health data through portable, persistent, and protected personal health records. Over time, person-centered data should empower individuals to shape how their data are used. 33. Both the benefits and risks of data are heightened for key populations, making confidentiality and security paramount. Personally identifiable data should never be used beyond the caregiver and point of service access unless protected by clear policies and rights. 34. The HIV response has achieved significant progress over four decades, with treatment expanding to an estimated 28 million people of the 38 million living with HIV in 2021. However, challenges such as loss to follow-up from ART and the need to better understand new infections and missed prevention opportunities remain. 35. Routine data systems must evolve to rapidly identify epidemiologic patterns and service gaps requiring intervention. This includes improving testing strategies to enhance early diagnosis and treatment initiation, achieving the 95–95–95 targets, and sustaining gains in treatment access while addressing testing and prevention needs. 36. Routine programmatic health data collection has advanced with the development of digital health data systems, enabling the use of individual-level data to improve patient care and the accuracy of aggregate data for surveillance. However, maintaining security and confidentiality is critical, requiring additional protections for digital systems. 37. Interoperability, such as adopting international technical standards, is essential to ensure cohesive and efficient use of data from multiple sources. Digital health systems must be scaled up with safeguards to protect individuals whose data are collected. 38. Strategic information provides essential data for improving health services and outcomes. Analyzing data to identify problems and areas for focus is a key aspect of decision-making in the HIV response.
